title: Serve every being as Shiva
hookLine: a teacher hears the word compassion and stops the room: who are you to be compassionate?
tomorrow: bhakti: Radha in the spring forest

cards: A charity photo: someone well dressed hands a meal to someone who isn't. Both smile for the camera, and the picture still says who's above and who's below. Now a temple garden at Dakshineswar, near Calcutta, in the 1880s.

A small group of young men sits around their teacher, Ramakrishna, and someone mentions a teaching about showing compassion to all living beings. It sounds beautiful. And Ramakrishna, the story goes, stops the room.

teach.h: WHO ARE YOU TO SHOW COMPASSION?
teach.b: Compassion to beings? he says. Who are you to show compassion? You, a tiny creature, being kind to others as if from above?
Serve every being as Shiva himself. In Bengali the phrase is often given as shiva jnane jiva seva: serving living beings, knowing them as God.
In the room was a young man named Narendranath, who would become Swami Vivekananda.

teach.h: A YOUNG MAN SAW A GREAT LIGHT.
teach.b: As his fellow disciples told it, he walked out afterward and said something like: I've found a great light today, and if God lets me, I'll proclaim it everywhere. And he did.
When he founded the Ramakrishna Mission, he gave it a motto that joins two things: for one's own liberation, and for the good of the world.

The word seva is older than any of them, from a Sanskrit root that means to attend on, to honor, to serve. In a temple, seva is what you do for the image of God: bathing it, dressing it, offering food.
Ramakrishna pointed that same word outward. The hungry person in front of you gets the same care as the image in the shrine. Now look at the charity photo again.
There's no above and below. The one serving stands where a worshiper stands.
Seva isn't volunteering on the side of your spiritual life. On the karma road, it is the spiritual life.

how: Seva is practiced in Hindu temples as service to the deity and to devotees, cleaning, cooking and serving food, and the Ramakrishna Mission and many other Hindu organizations run hospitals, schools and relief work as seva, serving people as God.

o: pity shown from above to those in need
action, offered as service to God in others
a fee paid to a temple for its rituals

p: from a root: to attend on, to honor
serve beings, knowing them as God

s: Ramakrishna praised the idea of showing compassion from above
he asked, who are you to show compassion? serve beings as Shiva instead.
seva is also the word for service to God's image in a temple
bathing, dressing and offering food to the image are all seva.
the Ramakrishna Mission's motto is only about helping others
it joins one's own liberation with the good of the world.

games.q: you're one of Ramakrishna's young followers. someone praises 'compassion for all beings'. how does Ramakrishna respond?
o: yes, compassion is the highest thing.
who are you to show compassion? serve every being as Shiva.
games.why: not compassion from above, but service, seeing God in the one you serve. Vivekananda built a mission on it.

practice: Think of someone you'll likely help today in any small way, a kid, a coworker, a stranger at a counter, an aging parent, and notice any feeling of being above them, even slightly: the helper, the one who has it together.
Let it go with the out-breath, and picture serving them the way you'd offer something at a shrine: carefully, gladly, as if it were an honor. If you pray, you can ask to see God in them.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action. On the karma road's last stretch, the action is seva: service offered to beings as if to God.

orig.note: Sanskrit: service, attendance, worship; from sev, to attend on or honor.

carryVoice: Your line: serve every being as Shiva. Ramakrishna carried a temple word out into the street. Day three hundred seventeen.

sources.ref: Ramakrishna's words on 'compassion' and 'service to beings as Shiva' (Dakshineswar, c. 1884), as reported by his disciples
sources.work: Sri Ramakrishna, the Great Master (Swami Saradananda)
